note.note:
History and Physical (H&P – Detailed)

Consult Summary:  
32-year-old male plastic-surgery doctor with 1.5–2-month history of recurrent right-sided paresthesia and motor weakness now increasing in frequency; GP’s working diagnosis is transient ischaemic attacks (TIAs) and has arranged urgent TIA clinic referral.

History:
• Presenting complaint: “Weird” neurological episodes.  
• Onset/Duration: Began ~6–8 weeks ago; initially infrequent (≈weekly/monthly) → now a few times per day. Each episode lasts 3–4 days, then resolves completely.  
• Character & Distribution:  
  – Pins-and-needles and numbness confined to right hand.  
  – Subjective weakness of right arm and right leg; colleague has noticed abnormal gait during episodes.  
  – Difficulty holding a coffee cup and transient sensation of “something in throat” (mild bulbar involvement) only during episodes.  
• Associated/constitutional: Fatigue, generalized weakness, intermittent nausea during episodes. No headaches, speech difficulty, or visual disturbance.  
• Exacerbating/relieving factors: None identified; spontaneous onset and resolution.  
• Current status: Asymptomatic at time of consult.

Pertinent negatives: No constant deficits; no dysarthria, diplopia, or swallowing difficulty outside episodes; no known prior strokes/TIAs.

Past Medical History:
• No chronic medical conditions reported.  
• Screening labs (BP, cholesterol, diabetes) “all OK” after father’s surgery.

Medications:
• Aspirin 75 mg once daily (self-initiated; route not documented).  
• No other regular medicines.  
Allergies: Penicillin (reaction details not discussed).

Social History:
• Occupation: Plastic-surgery doctor.  
• Lives with wife; has private place to speak.  
• Never smoked; alcohol/substance use not discussed.  
• No financial limitations mentioned.

Family History:
• Father: Carotid endarterectomy for stroke prevention (positive cerebrovascular disease history).  
• No other familial conditions recorded.

Physical Examination:
Vitals: Not recorded (remote video consult).  
General/Neurologic: No deficits observed during call (patient asymptomatic).  
Other systems: Not examined.

Investigations:
• None to date.  
• Planned: Urgent TIA clinic evaluation within 1–2 days for carotid Doppler ultrasound and possible brain imaging (CT/MRI).

Assessment & Plan:

Overall Impression: Recurrent unilateral sensory-motor episodes concerning for transient ischaemic attacks; alternative demyelinating or migraine aetiologies need exclusion.

DDx Integration:  
1. Recurrent TIA – unilateral episodes, complete recovery, family history; however episode length (>24 h) atypical but still prioritized by GP.  
2. Relapsing-remitting Multiple Sclerosis – young age, episodes lasting days, mixed motor-sensory features; opposing: strictly right-sided distribution and very rapid episode frequency.  
3. Hemiplegic/complex migraine – nausea and transient neuro deficits; opposing: absence of headache and prolonged duration.

Issue 1: Recurrent focal neurological episodes (suspected TIA)  
• Plan:  
  – Urgent referral to TIA clinic (sent today); expected appointment within 48 h (Thu/Fri).  
  – Tests anticipated: carotid Doppler ultrasound, brain imaging, other stroke-work-up.  
  – Safety-net: If symptoms recur and are prolonged, attend Emergency Department immediately.  
  – Contact GP for any delay or if unable to attend appointment; clinic and PALS numbers provided.

Issue 2: Self-prescribed Aspirin use  
• Assessment: Patient taking low-dose aspirin without prior medical advice.  
• Plan: No change documented in consult; TIA clinic to review continuation/risks.

General plan items:  
• Patient may telephone GP for interim advice.  
• Documentation of referral and contact details placed in record.

Quality checks:
• Missing elements: No vitals, physical exam limited by remote setting; alcohol intake not discussed.  
• No transcript–DDx conflicts noted (GP impression aligns with TIA while DDx adds MS as alternative).  
• Transcript quality: Occasional audio dropouts but clinically adequate; some initial confusion about asthma (resolved).
